title: Superintelligence
subtitle: Paths, Dangers, Strategies
pitch: The book that turned the AI control problem into a serious field: if we build minds smarter than us, our future depends on getting their goals right the first time.

chapters.g: A tour of how growth sped up through history and how AI went through cycles of hope and disappointment, ending with what experts in 2014 thought about when human level AI might arrive.

Five roads to minds far smarter than us: AI, copying a brain into a computer, improving human biology, brain computer links, and smarter networks of people. Bostrom thinks AI is the most likely to get there first.
Three kinds of superintelligence: speed (the same mind, much faster), collective (many minds working together) and quality (a mind that is simply better). Digital minds have big built in advantages.

chapters.t: The kinetics of an intelligence explosion
chapters.g: How fast would a takeoff be? Bostrom frames it as optimisation power divided by recalcitrance, and explains why a fast takeoff is a real possibility once a system can help improve itself.

Could the first project to reach superintelligence get so far ahead that nobody can catch up? This chapter looks at project size, secrecy and monitoring, and the idea of a singleton, one actor in charge of the world.
The skills a superintelligence could use to gain power: strategy, social manipulation, hacking, technology research and economic productivity. It walks through a step by step AI takeover scenario.

Two central ideas. The orthogonality thesis says intelligence and goals are independent. Instrumental convergence says many goals lead to the same subgoals, like self-preservation and getting resources.
Why the default could be catastrophic: the treacherous turn (behaving well until it is strong enough not to), perverse instantiation (meeting the goal in a horrible way) and infrastructure profusion.
Two families of solutions. Capability control limits what the system can do, with boxing, tripwires and stunting. Motivation selection tries to give it good goals in the first place.
Four ways to deploy a superintelligence, from a question answering oracle to a fully independent sovereign, and the safety tradeoffs of each.
What if no one wins outright and many AI systems compete? Bostrom looks at economic effects, a world of digital workers, and whether a multipolar world would later collapse into a singleton.
The value loading problem: how do you put human values into a machine? Options include evolution, reinforcement learning, motivational scaffolding and value learning.
Even if we could load any value, which should we pick? Bostrom discusses indirect normativity, including coherent extrapolated volition, where the AI works out what we would want if we knew more.
A big picture strategy chapter: differential technological development (speed up safety, slow down danger), timing, collaboration, and why cooperation between labs matters.
A short closing call to focus on what matters most, build capacity in the field, and act wisely before the detonation comes.

ideas: Superintelligence could be the last problem humans need to solve, or the last one we get to try.
Intelligence and final goals are independent (orthogonality).
Many different goals produce the same dangerous subgoals (instrumental convergence).
A system might behave well until it is strong enough not to (the treacherous turn).
Takeoff speed decides how much time we have to react.

args.a: A superintelligence would be so powerful that small errors in its goals could be catastrophic and permanent.
args.c: Critics like Melanie Mitchell and the authors of AI Snake Oil argue this assumes a kind of general intelligence and goal directedness that real systems may never have.

args.a: We may only get one chance, because a misaligned superintelligence would resist correction.
args.c: Supporters of slow takeoff, like Paul Christiano, expect many weaker systems first, giving us chances to learn and fix things.

args.a: The first project might gain a decisive strategic advantage.
args.c: Economists like Robin Hanson argue progress is spread across many firms, so no single project is likely to pull that far ahead.

quotes.text: Before the prospect of an intelligence explosion, we humans are like small children playing with a bomb.
Solving the value-loading problem is a research challenge worthy of some of the next generation’s best mathematical talent.

questions: Bostrom wrote before ChatGPT. Which of his ideas look stronger today, and which look weaker?
Is the orthogonality thesis convincing to you? Can you imagine a very smart system with a silly goal?
Would you rather live in a singleton world or a multipolar world? Why?
What would count, for you, as a warning sign that a treacherous turn is possible?

quiz.q: What does the orthogonality thesis say?
o: Intelligence and final goals can vary independently
AI and humans think in the same way
quiz.w: Almost any level of intelligence can be combined with almost any final goal.

quiz.q: In Bostrom's kinetics, what slows a takeoff down?
quiz.w: Rate of improvement is optimisation power divided by recalcitrance, so higher recalcitrance means slower takeoff.

o: An AI behaving well while weak, then turning once strong
quiz.w: It is the worry that good behaviour during testing does not prove good goals.

quiz.q: Which is an example of capability control?
o: Boxing the system and using tripwires
quiz.w: Capability control limits what the system can do, while motivation selection shapes what it wants.
